مرز میان دو ستون آخر مرزِ دانستن است. پراکسی معکوس دربارهٔ انتقال تصمیم می‌گیرد و چیزی از معنای کسب‌وکار نمی‌داند؛ دروازهٔ API — که مدخل خودش را در موضوع معماری دارد — دربارهٔ محتوا هم تصمیم می‌گیرد و برای همین است که آن مدخل هشدار می‌دهد هرچه بیشتر بداند بیشتر گلوگاه می‌شود. و مدخل سرویس مش، باز در همان موضوع، همین مسئله را برای ترافیک میان سرویس‌ها حل می‌کند نه برای ترافیک ورودی. هر سه لازم‌اند یا هیچ‌کدام لازم نیستند؛ چیزی که نباید کرد این است که یکی را وادار کنی کار دیگری را بکند.

دام رایج: پراکسی تک‌نمونه‌ای روی یک گره. این اشتباه از یک منطق درست شروع می‌شود. پراکسی حالا مرزِ ورودی است و همه‌چیز از آن رد می‌شود، پس آدم می‌خواهد سرِ جایش بماند و کنترل‌شده باشد؛ نتیجه‌اش این می‌شود که با یک نمونه و یک قید جای‌گذاری روی یک ماشین مشخص مستقر می‌شود. حالا آن ماشین نقطهٔ شکست واحد است — و بدترین نوعش، چون افتادنش کل کلاستر را از دسترس خارج می‌کند در حالی که هر سرویسِ دیگری سالم و در حال اجراست. همان‌طور که در مدخل خودترمیمی دیدیم سوارم تسک را جای دیگری بازسازی می‌کند، ولی قیدِ جای‌گذاری دقیقاً جلوی همین را گرفته است.

راه درست همان الگوی بالاست: سراسری، روی هر ماشین یکی، و آدرس همهٔ ماشین‌ها در DNS یا در متعادل‌کنندهٔ بیرونی. آن‌وقت افتادن یک ماشین فقط یک مقصد را از فهرست کم می‌کند.

و یک نکتهٔ آخر که کل این مرحله را می‌بندد: پراکسی معکوس جایگزین مش مسیریابی نیست، لایه‌ای بالای آن است — یا دقیق‌تر، کنارش. مش مسیریابی مسئلهٔ «کدام ماشین» را حل کرد و پراکسی مسئلهٔ «چه کاری با درخواست». هیچ‌کدام کار دیگری را نمی‌کند، و کلاستری که هر دو را دارد همان چیزی است که در عمل کار می‌کند.
fa.example:
قطعهٔ فایل استکِ یک پراکسی لبه. هر سه ویژگی‌ای که در بدنه گفتیم در آن دیده می‌شود:

services:

  edge:
    image: registry.example.com/edge-proxy:v2.0.0
    networks: [frontend]
    configs:
      - source: edge_routes
        target: /etc/edge/routes.yml
    deploy:
      mode: global
      update_config:
        order: stop-first
    ports:
      - target: 80
        published: 80
        mode: host
      - target: 443
        published: 443
        mode: host

  shop_api:
    image: registry.example.com/shop-api:v3.2.0
    networks: [frontend, backend]
    deploy:
      replicas: 3

  reporting:
    image: registry.example.com/reporting:v1.4.0
    networks: [frontend, backend]
    deploy:
      replicas: 2

networks:
  frontend:
    driver: overlay
  backend:
    driver: overlay

دو سرویس پشتی هیچ پورتی منتشر نکرده‌اند و از بیرون دیده نمی‌شوند. پراکسی از راه شبکهٔ مشترک به هر دو می‌رسد و پیکربندی مسیرهایش فقط نام سرویس دارد:

# /etc/edge/routes.yml
routes:
  - host: shop.example.com
    upstream: http://shop_api:8080
  - host: shop.example.com
    path: /reports
    upstream: http://reporting:8080

هیچ آدرسی و هیچ عدد پورتی از بیرون در این فایل نیست. حالا فهرست سرویس‌ها را ببین:

$ docker stack services shop
ID             NAME             MODE         REPLICAS   IMAGE                                     PORTS
mdcyhmn6v0va   shop_edge        global       3/3        registry.example.com/edge-proxy:v2.0.0
i1aehad5db9f   shop_shop_api    replicated   3/3        registry.example.com/shop-api:v3.2.0
vkbp6lpm4wz7   shop_reporting   replicated   2/2        registry.example.com/reporting:v1.4.0

ستون پورت‌ها برای هر سه خالی است. برای دو سرویس پشتی چون چیزی منتشر نکرده‌اند، و برای پراکسی چون پورتش را در حالت میزبان گرفته و به تسک تعلق دارد نه به سرویس:

$ docker service ps shop_edge --format "table {{.Node}}\t{{.CurrentState}}\t{{.Ports}}"
NODE      CURRENT STATE           PORTS
germany   Running 6 minutes ago   *:80->80/tcp,*:443->443/tcp
italy     Running 6 minutes ago   *:80->80/tcp,*:443->443/tcp
france    Running 6 minutes ago   *:80->80/tcp,*:443->443/tcp

و آدرس واقعی کاربر تا خودِ سرویس پشتی می‌رسد، چون پراکسی آن را در سرآیند می‌گذارد:

$ curl -s -H "Host: shop.example.com" http://italy/ | grep -E "RemoteAddr|X-Forwarded-For"
RemoteAddr: 10.0.3.7:41022
X-Forwarded-For: 203.0.113.44

آن RemoteAddr حالا آدرس خودِ پراکسی است، که طبیعی است — و آدرس کاربر در سرآیندی نشسته که پراکسی گذاشته. همان چیزی که مش مسیریابی به‌تنهایی نمی‌توانست بدهد، چون درخواست را باز نمی‌کند.

en.title: Reverse Proxy
en.short: A service at the cluster's edge doing what the routing mesh cannot: TLS, host and path routing, and the client's real address
en.body:
A reverse proxy is a service that sits at the cluster's edge and does what the routing mesh does not: terminating TLS, routing by hostname and path, rate limiting, and delivering the client's real address to the services.

The word "reverse" marks a distinction worth a sentence. An ordinary proxy acts on behalf of the client: the browser tells it what it wants and it reaches the world. A reverse proxy acts on behalf of the server: the world reaches it and it decides which service a request goes to. From the client's point of view there is no proxy at all; it sees one address and that address answers.

Why it is needed, in one sentence: in the Routing Mesh entry we saw that that machinery solves exactly one problem — "which machine do I write into my external load balancer" — and leaves the rest of the incoming-traffic problems unsolved. The table in that entry listed four unmet expectations. The reverse proxy is those four rows.

The mechanism in Swarm. The common and effective shape is this: a global service publishing ports eighty and four hundred and forty-three in host mode, reaching everything else internally by service name. Each of those three parts has a reason and we have met all three in this stage.

It is global because, as we saw in the Global Service entry, "one on every machine" is a rule and not a number; a machine added tomorrow takes a proxy of its own and no file changes. It is in host mode because, as we saw in the Host-Mode Publishing entry, that is the only way the client's real address reaches it — and if the proxy does not see the real address, no layer anywhere in the cluster ever will. And it works by name internally because, as we saw in the Service Discovery entry, a service name is the most stable thing in a cluster.

And a saving that is felt early: with this pattern the whole cluster publishes exactly two ports. As we saw in the Published Port entry, the outside port is unique across the cluster, and without this pattern every new service takes a number from a hand-kept list. With a proxy, a new service wants no port at all; it gets one block in the proxy's configuration and is reached by its name.

A bad example: every service on its own number. It always starts harmlessly — one service on 8081, the next on 8082, the third on 8083. After five services the port list gets written down somewhere; after ten, that list goes stale; and meanwhile other things become necessary. A TLS certificate has to be installed separately on every port, or cannot be, and the connection stays unencrypted. The addresses you hand to users carry port numbers in them, and changing them means changing everything that points at them. And nowhere can you say "every request under this path goes to that service", because the boundaries are ports and a port does not understand paths.

The mistake in that example was not the ports; it was that the system's entry boundary became as many points as there were services instead of one. A reverse proxy makes that boundary one again.

Which job belongs to what. These three are frequently confused with one another:

ResponsibilityRouting meshReverse proxyAPI gateway
getting a packet to a live taskyesyesyes
terminating TLSnoyesyes
routing by hostname and pathnoyesyes
delivering the client address to the servicenoyesyes
authentication and authorisationnousually notyes
composing several services into one answernonoyes

The line between the last two columns is a line of knowing. A reverse proxy decides about transport and knows nothing of business meaning; an API gateway — which has its own entry in the architecture topic — decides about content too, and that is why that entry warns that the more it knows, the more of a bottleneck it becomes. And the Service Mesh entry, again in that topic, solves this same problem for traffic between services rather than for incoming traffic. All three are needed or none of them are; what you must not do is force one to do another's job.

The common trap: a single-instance proxy on one node. This mistake starts from correct reasoning. The proxy is now the entry boundary and everything passes through it, so one wants it to stay put and be controlled; the result is a deployment with one replica and a placement constraint pinning it to a particular machine. Now that machine is a single point of failure — and the worst kind, because its falling takes the whole cluster out of reach while every other service is healthy and running. As we saw in the Self-Healing entry, Swarm rebuilds a task elsewhere, but the placement constraint is precisely what prevents that.

The right way is the pattern above: global, one per machine, with every machine's address in DNS or in the external load balancer. Then one machine falling merely removes one destination from a list.

And a last point that closes this whole stage: a reverse proxy does not replace the routing mesh, it is a layer above it — or more precisely, beside it. The routing mesh solved "which machine" and the proxy solves "what to do with the request". Neither does the other's job, and a cluster that has both is what actually works in practice.
en.example:
A fragment of an edge proxy's stack file. All three properties described in the body are visible in it:

services:

  edge:
    image: registry.example.com/edge-proxy:v2.0.0
    networks: [frontend]
    configs:
      - source: edge_routes
        target: /etc/edge/routes.yml
    deploy:
      mode: global
      update_config:
        order: stop-first
    ports:
      - target: 80
        published: 80
        mode: host
      - target: 443
        published: 443
        mode: host

  shop_api:
    image: registry.example.com/shop-api:v3.2.0
    networks: [frontend, backend]
    deploy:
      replicas: 3

  reporting:
    image: registry.example.com/reporting:v1.4.0
    networks: [frontend, backend]
    deploy:
      replicas: 2

networks:
  frontend:
    driver: overlay
  backend:
    driver: overlay

The two services behind it publish no port and are invisible from outside. The proxy reaches both over the shared network, and its route configuration carries only service names:

# /etc/edge/routes.yml
routes:
  - host: shop.example.com
    upstream: http://shop_api:8080
  - host: shop.example.com
    path: /reports
    upstream: http://reporting:8080

No address and no external port number appears in that file. Now look at the service list:

$ docker stack services shop
ID             NAME             MODE         REPLICAS   IMAGE                                     PORTS
mdcyhmn6v0va   shop_edge        global       3/3        registry.example.com/edge-proxy:v2.0.0
i1aehad5db9f   shop_shop_api    replicated   3/3        registry.example.com/shop-api:v3.2.0
vkbp6lpm4wz7   shop_reporting   replicated   2/2        registry.example.com/reporting:v1.4.0

The ports column is empty for all three. For the two services behind because they publish nothing, and for the proxy because its port is taken in host mode and belongs to the task rather than the service:

$ docker service ps shop_edge --format "table {{.Node}}\t{{.CurrentState}}\t{{.Ports}}"
NODE      CURRENT STATE           PORTS
germany   Running 6 minutes ago   *:80->80/tcp,*:443->443/tcp
italy     Running 6 minutes ago   *:80->80/tcp,*:443->443/tcp
france    Running 6 minutes ago   *:80->80/tcp,*:443->443/tcp

And the client's real address reaches the service behind, because the proxy puts it in a header:

$ curl -s -H "Host: shop.example.com" http://italy/ | grep -E "RemoteAddr|X-Forwarded-For"
RemoteAddr: 10.0.3.7:41022
X-Forwarded-For: 203.0.113.44

That RemoteAddr is now the proxy's own address, which is as it should be — and the client's address sits in a header the proxy set. Exactly what the routing mesh alone could not give, because it never opens the request.
